nameStory: The White Hake gets its name from its pale, whitish coloration that distinguishes it from its darker relatives. The alternative name 'mud hake' comes from its habit of living near muddy bottoms in deeper waters, where it hunts for food along the seafloor.
description: The White Hake is a bottom-dwelling fish found in the deeper, cooler waters off New England's coast. It has an elongated body with a tapering tail and belongs to the cod family, sharing some similarities with its more famous cousin. These fish typically grow to moderate sizes and have a distinctly pale appearance compared to other hake species. They prefer the deeper waters of the northwest Atlantic, making them less commonly encountered by casual anglers.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale whitish to light gray coloration overall, giving it a distinctly lighter appearance than other hakes - the body feels smooth and somewhat slimy to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Elongated, torpedo-shaped body that tapers toward the tail, with a somewhat compressed profile that feels firm when handled

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Two dorsal fins on the back with the second one being longer, and a single long anal fin - the fins have a translucent quality

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Terminal mouth (opens at the front tip of the head) with small teeth that feel rough against your finger

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in deeper offshore waters over muddy or sandy bottoms, rarely encountered in shallow coastal areas

habitat: White Hake live in the deeper waters off New England's coast, typically over muddy or sandy bottoms in the continental shelf waters. They prefer cooler temperatures found in these offshore depths, usually beyond the reach of most recreational shore fishing. You're most likely to encounter them through deep-sea fishing charters or commercial fishing operations.

seasonality.spring: Begin moving toward spawning areas in deeper waters, becoming more active as water temperatures start to rise.
seasonality.summer: Peak spawning season when adults may be found in slightly shallower waters, though still well offshore.
seasonality.fall: Adults disperse back to deeper waters as temperatures cool, with young fish beginning to establish in their preferred muddy bottom habitats.
seasonality.winter: Remain in deeper, more stable temperature waters where they continue feeding along the muddy seafloor.

funFact: White Hake can actually 'walk' along the seafloor using modified pelvic fins that act like little legs, helping them navigate through the muddy bottom terrain where they hunt for buried prey!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Red Hake, but White Hake are noticeably paler and prefer deeper waters. Remember: 'White and deep, Red and shallow' - Red Hake are more reddish-brown and often found in shallower coastal waters.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'hake,' this fish is actually in a different family (Phycidae) than true hakes, though they're closely related within the cod order. The 'phycid hake' designation helps distinguish this group from other hake families.
compareHints: White Hake is the palest of the three Urophycis species in New England waters - much lighter than the reddish-brown Red Hake and lacking the distinctive spots of the Spotted Hake. It also prefers the deepest waters of the three, while Red Hake often ventures into shallower coastal areas and Spotted Hake typically stays in intermediate depths.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Red hake can be distinguished from their close relatives by color - they're much more reddish than the grayish white hake or the spotted pattern of spotted hake.
Unlike red hake which has a reddish tint and white hake which is more uniformly colored, spotted hake is the only one in the genus with distinct dark spots.
